source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite probability space
statement: A finite probability model assigns nonnegative probabilities to elementary outcomes whose total is one; an event probability is the sum over its outcomes.
conclusion: P is normalized, nonnegative, and additive on disjoint events.
typical_uses: Build a correct sample space before counting.
common_misuses: Treating unordered outcomes as equally likely when ordered outcomes are not.
repair_templates: List elementary outcomes and verify their probabilities sum to one.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Complement rule
statement: For any event A, P(A complement)=1-P(A).
conditions: A is an event in a probability space.
conclusion: The probability of an event can be computed from its complement.
bridge_lemmas: A and its complement partition the sample space.
repair_templates: Rewrite the target as the complement of a simpler event.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Addition rule
statement: P(A union B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A intersection B); for disjoint events the intersection term is zero.
conclusion: Union probabilities are obtained by inclusion-exclusion for two events.
typical_uses: Handle overlapping cases without double counting.
common_misuses: Adding probabilities of non-disjoint events directly.
bridge_lemmas: Partition A union B into A minus B, B minus A, and the intersection.
repair_templates: Subtract the overlap or partition into disjoint cases.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Conditional product rule
statement: P(A intersection B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A) whenever the conditioning probability is positive.
conditions: A and B are events and the relevant conditioning event has positive probability.
conclusion: Joint probabilities factor into conditional and marginal probabilities.
bridge_lemmas: Conditional probability is defined by P(A|B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B).
repair_templates: Write the conditioning event explicitly in the denominator.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Bayes rule
statement: For a partition {B_i} with positive probabilities, P(B_j|A)=P(A|B_j)P(B_j)/sum_i P(A|B_i)P(B_i).
conditions: The B_i form a finite or countable partition and P(A)>0.
conclusion: Posterior probabilities are proportional to likelihood times prior.
typical_uses: Reverse conditional probabilities in diagnostic and classification problems.
common_misuses: Using P(A|B) as P(B|A) without normalization.
bridge_lemmas: Law of total probability for the denominator.
repair_templates: Expand P(A) over the partition before dividing.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Law of total probability
statement: If {B_i} partitions the sample space, then P(A)=sum_i P(A|B_i)P(B_i).
conditions: The B_i are pairwise disjoint and cover the sample space.
conclusion: A probability decomposes into conditional probabilities over a partition.
typical_uses: Compute mixture probabilities and Bayes denominators.
bridge_lemmas: A is the disjoint union of A intersection B_i.
repair_templates: Check partition coverage and disjointness first.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Binomial distribution
statement: The number of successes in n independent Bernoulli trials with success probability p has probability mass C(n,k)p^k(1-p)^(n-k).
conditions: Trials are independent and identically distributed with two outcomes.
typical_uses: Model counts of successes and derive approximations.
common_misuses: Applying it when trial probabilities differ or dependence is present.
bridge_lemmas: Choose the k success positions and multiply independent probabilities.
repair_templates: Verify identical p and independence before using the formula.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Linearity of expectation
statement: For integrable random variables, E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c without requiring independence.
conclusion: Expectation distributes over finite linear combinations.
common_misuses: Adding variances as if expectation required independence.
bridge_lemmas: Expectation is a finite or absolutely convergent sum/integral.
repair_templates: Use linearity directly and reserve independence for products.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Indicator variable method
statement: For an event A, E[1_A]=P(A); sums of indicators count how many component events occur.
conditions: A is an event and indicators are integrable.
typical_uses: Count expected numbers of occurrences without independence.
common_misuses: Assuming indicators must be independent for linearity.
bridge_lemmas: An indicator takes values zero and one.
repair_templates: Express the count as a sum of indicators.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Variance and covariance expansion
conclusion: Variance measures centered second moment and includes covariance cross terms.
typical_uses: Compute dispersion of sums and diagnose dependence.
common_misuses: Dropping covariance without independence or zero covariance.
repair_templates: Expand the square and retain covariance terms.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Variance of independent sums
statement: If X_i are pairwise independent with finite variances, Var(sum_i X_i)=sum_i Var(X_i).
conditions: The variables have finite second moments and pairwise independence.
repair_templates: State pairwise independence or retain covariance terms.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Convolution formula
statement: For independent discrete X,Y, P(X+Y=n)=sum_k P(X=k)P(Y=n-k); continuous densities convolve by an integral.
conclusion: The distribution of a sum is the convolution of the component distributions.
typical_uses: Derive distributions of sums and random walks.
bridge_lemmas: Partition the event X+Y=n by values of X.
repair_templates: Condition on one summand and invoke independence.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Weak law of large numbers
statement: For iid variables with finite mean and variance, the sample average converges in probability to the common mean.
conditions: X_i are iid with finite variance and mean mu.
conclusion: P(|n^{-1}sum_i X_i-mu|>epsilon) tends to zero for every epsilon>0.
typical_uses: Justify frequency stabilization and statistical estimation.
common_misuses: Claiming almost sure convergence from this statement alone.
bridge_lemmas: Chebyshev inequality applied to the sample mean.
repair_templates: Specify convergence mode and moment assumptions.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Chebyshev inequality
statement: For finite-variance X, P(|X-E X|>=a) <= Var(X)/a^2 for a>0.
conditions: X has finite mean and variance.
conclusion: Large deviations from the mean have a variance-controlled upper bound.
typical_uses: Prove convergence in probability and tail bounds.
common_misuses: Using a one-sided or strict inequality without checking the event form.
repair_templates: Square the deviation and use Markov's inequality.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Central limit theorem
statement: For iid variables with mean mu and variance sigma squared>0, the standardized sum converges in distribution to a standard normal law.
conditions: X_i are iid with finite nonzero variance.
conclusion: (sum_i X_i-n mu)/(sigma sqrt n) converges in distribution to N(0,1).
typical_uses: Approximate probabilities for large sums and sample means.
common_misuses: Using it for dependent variables or without scaling by sqrt n.
bridge_lemmas: Standardization and continuity correction for lattice variables.
repair_templates: Check iid/moment assumptions and use the correct normalization.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Probability generating function
statement: For a nonnegative integer-valued X, G_X(s)=E[s^X] encodes its mass function; independent sums multiply generating functions.
conditions: X takes values in nonnegative integers and the series is defined near s=0.
conclusion: Coefficients recover probabilities and G_{X+Y}=G_X G_Y under independence.
typical_uses: Solve recurrence distributions and branching processes.
common_misuses: Confusing ordinary generating functions with moment generating functions.
bridge_lemmas: Coefficient extraction from the power series.
repair_templates: State the support and independence before multiplying PGFs.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Transition matrix and Markov property
statement: A finite Markov chain has transition probabilities p_ij=P(X_{n+1}=j|X_n=i) depending only on the current state; each row sums to one.
conditions: The state space is finite and conditional probabilities are defined.
conclusion: The distribution evolves by multiplication with the transition matrix.
typical_uses: Model stochastic dynamics and compute multi-step probabilities.
common_misuses: Using a matrix with columns summing to one under a row-vector convention.
repair_templates: Fix row/column convention and verify stochastic normalization.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Absorbing-chain fundamental matrix
statement: For transient submatrix Q of an absorbing finite chain, N=(I-Q)^{-1}=sum_{n>=0}Q^n gives expected visit counts before absorption.
conditions: The chain has absorbing states and Q describes transient-to-transient transitions.
conclusion: Absorption probabilities and expected times follow from N and the transient-to-absorbing block.
typical_uses: Solve gambler's ruin and expected absorption problems.
common_misuses: Inverting I-Q when the transient block is not truly transient.
bridge_lemmas: Geometric matrix series converges when spectral radius(Q)<1.
repair_templates: Reorder states into transient and absorbing blocks first.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Gambler's ruin probabilities
statement: For a biased nearest-neighbor walk on {0,...,N}, the probability of hitting N before 0 from i is (1-(q/p)^i)/(1-(q/p)^N) when p is not q, and i/N when p=q.
conditions: Steps are independent with up probability p and down probability q=1-p; 0 and N are absorbing.
conclusion: The hitting probability solves the harmonic recurrence h_i=p h_{i+1}+q h_{i-1} with boundary values 0 and 1.
common_misuses: Using the biased formula at p=q without taking the limit.
repair_templates: Set up the recurrence and treat p=q separately.
